hints: Focus on the three conditions that must all be true at once, that X really does have the higher first ionisation energy, plus which student statement is factually true.
Check each pair for proton number and for size, remembering radius decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Look for the pair where the higher ionisation energy cannot be explained by more protons, but can be explained by a closer electron to the nucleus.
walkthrough:
**Recall what controls first ionisation energy**

First ionisation energy depends on nuclear charge, atomic radius (distance of outer electron) and shielding. More protons pulls harder, smaller radius pulls harder.

$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + e^{-} \quad \Delta H = \text{1st IE}$$

**Translate the two student statements**

Student 1 is correct only if proton number of X > proton number of Y. Student 2 is correct only if atomic radius of X < atomic radius of Y. We need X with higher IE than Y, but only one statement factually true.

**Test the Period 2 anomalies**

Carbon has higher IE than boron and more protons and smaller radius, so both students are right. Magnesium has higher IE than aluminium, but Mg has fewer protons ($12 < 13$) and larger radius than Al, so both students are wrong. Oxygen has lower IE than nitrogen because of paired electron repulsion in $2p$, so the starting premise fails.

**Test oxygen and sulfur**

Oxygen does have higher first IE than sulfur ($1314 > 1000 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ approx) because the outer electron is in n=2 with much less shielding and much closer to the nucleus. Proton number of O ($8$) is less than S ($16$), so student 1 is wrong. Radius of O is smaller than S (up the group), so student 2 is right. Only one student is correct, which fits perfectly.

options.A: Carbon does have higher first IE than boron, but both students are correct here. Carbon has more protons (6 > 5) and a smaller atomic radius across Period 2, so this gives two correct students, not one.
options.B: Magnesium does have higher first IE than aluminium due to the stable 3s2 subshell, but both students are incorrect. Mg has fewer protons than Al (12 < 13) and a larger atomic radius across Period 3, so neither explanation is factually true.
options.C: This pair fails the first premise. Nitrogen has higher first IE than oxygen due to spin-pair repulsion in oxygen's paired 2p electron. So X does not have higher IE than Y, even though both proton and radius statements would be factually true.
options.D: Oxygen has higher first IE than sulfur because its outer electron is closer to the nucleus with less shielding down the group. Student 1 is wrong because O has fewer protons than S, but student 2 is right because O is smaller than S. This gives exactly one correct student.
